items.title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.original_title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.summary: Look at it from the viewpoint of a shipper moving goods by containership on the Asia-Europe route. The proportion of ships on this route which arrived on the scheduled day of arrival declined from 51% in May to just 31% in September (average of all ports and all carriers), according to the Drewry Container Capacity Insight. Even the Gemini alliance, which has a higher-than-average track record for on-time arrivals, managed just 34% in September. The Asia-Europe trade’s schedule reliability scores by carrier in September ranged between 19% and 38% and the proportion of sailings not cancelled ranged between 0% and 23%, according to Drewry’s analysis for this route. Looking at this from a carrier viewpoint, the logic is that cargo volumes were strong in the peak season, port congestion got worse in Asia, but the carriers could make higher profits by throwing more ship capacity at the market and cancelling fewer sailings… which must have made port congestion worse. At Drewry, we are looking more closely at how carrier performance, port congestion and network exposure can be brought together to give shippers a clearer picture of where they may be vulnerable. Ultimately, the aim should be to move away from simply reacting to delays and towards building those risks into carrier selection, procurement strategies and contingency planning.

items.title: The Week in Alt Fuels: Building the bunker menu
items.original_title: The Week in Alt Fuels: Building the bunker menu
items.summary: Bunkering activity came in many flavours this week, with biofuels, LNG, LBM, methanol, ethanol and ammonia featuring across several major ports – and sometimes with multiple fuels at the same port. items.title: IEA Moves to Accelerate Oil Reserve Releases as Hormuz Crisis Drags On
items.original_title: IEA Moves to Accelerate Oil Reserve Releases as Hormuz Crisis Drags On
items.summary: The International Energy Agency (IEA) has agreed to accelerate the release of approximately 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as the prolonged Strait of Hormuz crisis continues to strain global energy supplies. The decision, announced Thursday following a meeting of the agency’s Governing Board, comes amid mounting concerns over diesel shortages, high fuel prices and renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Middle East. According to the IEA’s statement , member countries have already released approximately 330 million barrels under the emergency stock release agreed in March in response to the Iran war. The agency said it would take steps to accelerate the remaining releases, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to be made available as soon as possible. In its October Oil Market Report , published Wednesday, the IEA said disruptions to production and exports from the Middle East and Russia removed approximately 1.3 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil exports from the market in September compared with a year earlier. It forecasts global oil demand will decline by 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026 as higher prices and weaker economic activity take their toll.

items.summary: DHL Express has committed €300m in investment across Africa through to 2030, as the logistics group urges UK businesses to diversify supply chains and pursue opportunities in an area expected to become a major global growth engine by 2035. Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa, said the investment “reflected the company’s confidence in the continent’s long-term prospects”, amid shifting global trade relationships, geopolitical tensions, and changes to supply chains. “We would not commit to €300m if we didn’t believe in the future of this continent,” he said today. He said only 12% of African cities were connected by at least one commercial flight a week, underscoring the challenges facing companies seeking to expand manufacturing and distribution. DHL is looking to address some of these constraints through its existing network, which Mr Heymans said spanned every African country and territory. In sub-Saharan Africa, the company operates 12 dedicated aircraft, alongside road transport, facilities and other air connections. The executives stressed that businesses should not approach Africa as a single market, given the differences in languages, legal systems, currencies, and trade regulations. “Be specific to which countries in Africa you want to offer trade to,” Mr Heymans said, and advised companies to identify markets and sectors best suited to their products before expanding.

items.title: EU may need to cut winter gas demand by 7% with gas storage at a record seasonal low
items.original_title: EU may need to cut winter gas demand by 7% with gas storage at a record seasonal low
items.summary: Low levels of gas in storage leave the EU with less of a buffer against liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes being diverted to Asia, further disruption in the Middle East or the loss of Russian LNG from January 2027. The EU is heading into winter with gas storage about 72.4% full as of 3 October, the lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011. Together with the EU’s full ban on imports of Russian LNG from January 2027, this shortfall could require the bloc to cut winter gas demand by 7%, or 14bcm, compared with last winter. Gas demand creeps up as imports stay flat Before 2022, EU gas storage was a seasonal buffer: fill in summer, withdraw in winter, with flexible (mainly Russian) pipeline imports absorbing demand swings. Storage’s share of EU winter gas consumption rose from 25% in 2021–22 to 30% in 2025–26, with a five-year high of 33% in 2024–25, according to Eurostat. Winter gas consumption fell sharply from roughly 222bcm in 2021–22 to around 185bcm in 2022–23, as high prices and emergency gas-saving measures cut demand. In late September, the German government instructed state-owned gas importer SEFE to procure and store 8 terawatt-hours of gas, about 3% of the country’s storage capacity, by 15 December.

items.title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
items.original_title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
items.summary: The SMAP mechanism introduced under the ETS represents an opportunity to help the maritime sector to transition towards clean fuels and propulsion technologies, and strengthen Europe’s industrial leadership. With an estimated support of €15 billion between 2028 and 2040, such a mechanism could encourage shipping companies to use green e-fuels, which will need to be scaled up in this period to meet long-term decarbonisation targets. The European Commission’s Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) mentions that in less than a decade, 4.6 million tonnes of e-fuels could be needed to reach FuelEU targets. A high price difference coverage in favour of e-fuels compared to other alternative fuels under SMAP is a welcome step, but is unlikely to be sufficient in itself to ensure a genuine move towards e-fuels. Because of the capital-intensive nature of e-fuels production, these projects will require producers to enter long-term offtake agreements with companies in order to secure investment. The current SMAP proposal is unlikely to provide sufficient support to this process. While some alternative fuels and zero-emissions propulsion technologies have a role to play in reducing maritime GHG emissions, SMAP should be used primarily to reward long-term e-fuel use, rather than short-term fuel and propulsion technological options which may already be incentivised under existing legislation.

items.title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
items.original_title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
items.summary: A Korean-developed integrated design framework has been developed to comprehensively analyze “ship survivability”—a naval vessel’s ability to avoid enemy attack, withstand damage when hit, restore key functions after damage, and continue its mission. The key achievement is the integration of survivability analyses that had previously been performed using separate software tools into a single software environment. The AX Convergence Research Center of the Virtual Engineering Platform Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM, President Seog-Hyeon Ryu) developed ‘isSAFE,’ an integrated ship survivability design framework. isSAFE provides an integrated design environment in which a ship model can be built, various weapon hit scenarios can be generated, and vulnerability, recoverability, and results analyses can be performed in a continuous workflow. Ship survivability consists of three elements: susceptibility, the ability to avoid enemy detection and attack; vulnerability, the ability to withstand damage when hit; and recoverability, the ability to restore key functions after damage. This enables users to compare survivability under different ship configurations and conditions and is expected to support the Republic of Korea Navy (ROK Navy), shipyards, and other end users in ship design and survivability assessments.

items.title: Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong
items.original_title: Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong
items.summary: Greek tanker owner Liquimar Tankers has been linked to an order for three suezmax newbuildings in China, adding fresh crude carrier capacity after cashing in on the strong secondhand tanker market. The Dimitris Papadimitriou-controlled company has contracted three 157,000 dwt vessels at Jiangsu New Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, according to shipbuilding sources. The conventionally fuelled tankers are scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2030, with pricing estimated at just under $86m apiece, putting the potential investment at close to $258m. The pair changed hands for a reported $68m each, generating approximately $136m in gross sale proceeds. Liquimar has already emerged behind another Chinese tanker project this year. In August, shipbuilding intelligence identified the company as the owner of the 113,500 dwt aframax/LR2 Priamos under construction at Hengli Heavy Industries. Liquimar was set up in 1990, as a way for its parent company, Dioryx Maritime Corp, to expand from dry cargo and containerships into the oil tanker sector, before becoming a standalone entity in 1995. The latest reported deal would add another name to New Hantong’s suezmax orderbook. Earlier this year, Eyal Ofer’s Zodiac Maritime contracted four suezmaxes at the Chinese yard for 2029 delivery, taking its programme in the segment to nine vessels.

items.title: HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships
items.original_title: HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships
items.summary: South Korea’s HMM is pressing ahead with its fleet expansion programme, approving a $1.62bn investment in 12 containerships comprising eight 13,000 teu newbuildings and four smaller vessels. The Seoul-listed carrier’s board approved spending KRW2.168trn ($1.617bn) yesterday, according to a stock exchange filing. The investment includes fresh orders for eight 13,000 teu ships, alongside the acquisition of three 2,800 teu vessels and one 1,700 teu ship through resale transactions involving newbuildings already under construction. The 12 vessels will add a combined 114,100 teu of capacity, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by December 2029. HMM has yet to identify the shipyards responsible for the eight larger vessels or the sellers of the four smaller ships. Propulsion specifications have also not been disclosed. The latest investment follows last year’s KRW4trn ($2.8bn) commitment covering 12 LNG dual-fuel 13,000 teu containerships and two VLCCs, with HD Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean securing the boxship contracts. Under HMM’s business plan through to 2030, the carrier aims to expand its containership fleet to 166 vessels totalling 1.47m teu by the end of the decade, alongside 110 bulk carriers with a combined capacity of 13.52m dwt.

items.title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
items.original_title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
items.summary: West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September.

items.original_title: GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck
items.summary: Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a framework agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group, bringing the heavy-steel fabricator into its shipbuilding operations. GSI said its expanding orderbook and increasingly complex vessel mix would drive up demand for hull blocks over the coming years, prompting the move to bring in additional manufacturing capacity. A separate project launched in September will see a new facility built at Longxue North, with GSI lined up to operate the yard once completed in 2029. The China Railway Construction Corporation subsidiary is fabricating 10 cargo-hold bottom sections weighing up to 96 tonnes each, which are to be transported to Shanghai for final assembly. The company has established three outdoor block assembly lines and is targeting annual ship block production of up to 100,000 tonnes, with longer-term ambitions to move into complete vessel construction. Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding also proposed a new block fabrication and assembly facility last year to address capacity constraints and reduce its reliance on external subcontractors.

As regulatory and commercial pressures increase through measures such as FuelEU Maritime, the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction ambitions, retrofitting existing vessels is becoming an increasingly important pathway for owners seeking to improve efficiency, reduce emissions and extend asset life. To help the industry navigate these challenges, LR’s new publication brings together alternative fuels and energy-saving devices within a single retrofit framework. The guidance emphasises the importance of early collaboration between owners, shipyards, equipment manufacturers, flag administrations and classification societies to avoid delays and reduce project risk. When the US tight oil industry emerged in the 2010s, setting the country on course to become the world’s largest producer, there was a lot of speculation about how calculations around American energy security had changed forever. The US no longer needed to care about what happened in the Middle East, said some. A surge in US production that helps ease tightness in world oil markets and brings down prices would be one clear way for American consumers to benefit. On the other hand, expecting the US tight oil industry not to respond to higher prices would also be a mistake. Wood Mackenzie’s rule of thumb is that production typically takes about nine to 12 months to respond after prices have moved. That increased activity has led him to raise his forecasts for US Lower 48 oil production. items.title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.original_title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.summary: Terminals at Antwerp and Rotterdam are coming under growing pressure as unseasonably low water along the Rhine continues to restrict container barge movements on the river, with cargo being pushed towards already-constrained rail and road networks. SeasC4U’s Gunther Ginckels told The Loadstar barges around Duisburg-Ruhrort were operating at roughly two-thirds of normal capacity, while vessels further upstream were carrying substantially smaller loads. “Some services are suspended further upstream on the Kaub gauge, where low water has severely restricted navigation, while large volumes are being shifted to rail and truck, but alternative capacity is limited,” said Mr Ginckels. “Cargo is still moving, but carrying capacity is sharply reduced, transport costs have risen, transit times are longer and less predictable, while inland terminals, rail networks, and trucking markets are absorbing displaced cargo at higher cost and delays.” Some 35% of box movements along the Dutch hinterland tend to travel by inland waterway, meaning that even seeing a part of that traffic transferred to alternative modes piles massive pressure onto already constrained transport networks. Back in August, Metro Global stated that more than 200 trucks would be required to replace lost barge capacity, and while low water levels have become part and parcel of the Rhine’s summer months in recent years, the persisting into October presented additional problems.

items.title: NATO’s Black Sea flank on alert after series of attacks
items.original_title: NATO’s Black Sea flank on alert after series of attacks
items.summary: A chemical tanker has reported a suspected drone strike inside Romanian territorial waters. The Comoros-flagged Yara J was anchored approximately 10 nautical miles southeast of Sulina on Wednesday evening when its crew reported an explosion and fire onboard. The vessel, which was in ballast and reportedly preparing to enter the Danube, extinguished the fire without outside assistance. Unlike the previous attacks in the exclusive economic zones of Romania and Bulgaria, both NATO members, Wednesday’s incident occurred inside Romanian territorial waters. The latest incident follows five reported drone attacks on merchant shipping off the two countries since October 5, with three vessels sinking. It followed this morning with claims of attacks on two more dry cargo vessels bound for the Ukrainian port, alongside strikes against infrastructure at the Danube port of Izmail. Another drone was detected over Romanian territorial waters southeast of Sulina at 01.34 this morning, prompting further deployments of Spanish F-18s and Romanian F-16s. Bulgaria is working with Türkiye and Romania on an initiative to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea, foreign minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova announced in Berlin yesterday. Petrova-Chamova also highlighted plans to establish a Black Sea Maritime Security Centre, with operations in Varna and Constanța, to improve surveillance and protect critical infrastructure.

items.title: Capital Axis behind capesize deal of the year
items.original_title: Capital Axis behind capesize deal of the year
items.summary: Broking sources are reporting the highest-priced capesize vessel transaction of 2026, with Greek owner Capital Axis Maritime reportedly in the process of selling a newbuilding for $90m. Brokers report the Arriktos, a 181,250 dwt capesize under construction at China’s Hengli Shipbuilding, also known as Hengli Dalian Hl-B181k-25, is reportedly attracting Chinese buyers at $90m. The vessel, scheduled for delivery in October 2027, is valued at $82.95m by VesselsValue, which also records its sale from Hengli Petrochemical to Capital Axis Maritime for $74m in January. If concluded at the reported price, the latest transaction would represent a $16m increase, or nearly 22%, over the January acquisition price, highlighting the sharp appreciation in modern capesize asset values. Capital Axis Maritime is the Greek dry bulk venture established earlier this year through a partnership between Evangelos Marinakis-backed Capital Executive Ship Management and Nicholas E. In January, Greek owner Seanergy Maritime contracted a sister vessel for $75.2m, with delivery scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. The Arriktos resale, if concluded at $90m, would represent a premium of almost $15m over Seanergy’s January contract price,. The latest deal comes amid strengthening dry bulk asset values. Secondhand bulkcarrier prices have continued to gain ground, with Clarksons reporting a 5% increase in its overall index over the past two months.

items.title: LD Armateurs unveils world’s first six-sail cargo ship
items.original_title: LD Armateurs unveils world’s first six-sail cargo ship
items.summary: French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six Norsepower rotor sails on Spirit of Toulouse, creating what it says is the world’s first cargo vessel fitted with six mechanical sails. The ship, being built in China for Airbus logistics work, is the lead vessel in a three-ship series designed to transport large aircraft sub-assemblies between Europe and North America. LD Armateurs said the six 35 m by 5 m rotor sails had now been installed at a coastal outfitting site in Shanghai by Wuchang Shipbuilding Industry Group, ahead of upcoming sea trials. The installation gives Spirit of Toulouse the highest number of mechanical sails yet fitted to a commercial cargo ship, and makes it the largest roro vessel equipped with wind propulsion, according to the company and rotor sail supplier Norsepower. The wind-assist system will work alongside two dual-fuel main engines and two dual-fuel generator sets capable of running on e-methanol, bio-methanol or marine diesel oil. LD Armateurs said the combination of methanol capability and wind propulsion was designed to cut fuel consumption and emissions on the vessel’s transatlantic route rather than rely on a single decarbonisation technology. “Spirit of Toulouse is much more than a new vessel,” said Samira Draoua, chief executive of LD Armateurs.

items.title: EU economy chief doubtful Russian diesel exports will affect prices
items.original_title: EU economy chief doubtful Russian diesel exports will affect prices
items.summary: EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis told AFP on Tuesday that Russian diesel sales recently authorised by the United States were unlikely to move the price of the commodity, which has spiked since the start of the Iran war. Comparing the emissions performance of road, rail and shipping across four essential Australian freight routes, The Emission Reduction Potential of Mode Shift to Maritime Transport report found greenhouse gas emissions reductions of between 60 to 90 per cent by rebalancing freight between road and coastal shipping. Launched at Parliament House today by the Hon. Catherine King, the report was developed by Transport Emissions/Energy Research and commissioned by the Maritime Union of Australia in collaboration with Maritime Industry Australia Limited (MIAL) and supported by the Energy Futures Foundation. Clare Grandison, Principal Advisor – Decarbonisation and Industry Transformation, said the report shows significant diesel fuel use and emissions reductions are possible using today’s technology and maritime footprint. “The Australian transport sector is a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, making up more than 21 per cent of total emissions each year. The report shows emissions reductions are feasible now, using today’s vessels, infrastructure and capability.” Angela Gillham, CEO of MIAL, said the said greater use of coastal shipping could improve productivity for the freight sector and strengthen supply chain resilience.

REUTERS/Nacho Doce The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is proposing $200,000 fees on Spanish-flagged vessels entering American ports, along with restrictions on billions of dollars in Spanish imports, after concluding that Spain’s refusal to admit certain U.S.-flagged ships has created unfavorable conditions for American shipping. The proposed measures include a $200,000 fee each time a Spanish-flagged vessel enters a U.S. port from abroad, as well as potential restrictions on imports of Spanish cosmetics, oils and fats, ceramics, stone products, and sugar and confectionery. The dispute began in November 2024, when Spanish authorities refused port access to the U.S.-flagged Maersk Denver and Maersk Seletar , both operated by Maersk Line, Limited, over cargo connected to Israel. The regulator said the restrictions undermine the ability of U.S.-flagged ships to compete for cargo moving to and from Spain, while also affecting vessels that could be called upon to support U.S. The Commission has now narrowed its proposed vessel fee to $200,000 per voyage while identifying specific categories of Spanish goods that could face import restrictions. The FMC said the proposed penalties are intended to address shipping conditions created by Spain’s port restrictions, rather than the broader political dispute over the transportation of military cargo to Israel.

The Nasdaq-listed dry bulk owner is paying about $37m for the latest vessel, which is scheduled for delivery in the third quarter of 2029. EuroDry currently operates 11 bulkers totalling 766,420 dwt, including two kamsarmaxes, six supra/ultramaxes and three older panamaxes. On the current fleet count, delivery of all five ships would take EuroDry to 16 bulkers with around 1.14m dwt of capacity. items.summary: Cyber extortion group ‘n0n’ has named 38 organisations across the global shipping and ports sector on its dark-web leak site, raising concerns that data may have been stolen. Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar reported yesterday n0n published the listings in a single batch on 12 October, that included container terminals, shipping lines, port IT providers, and logistics businesses across 18 countries. The group emerged last month, listing 21 organisations across sectors including telecoms, retail, pharmaceuticals, and education. SOCRadar said the pattern of data described in the listings suggested a possible common point of entry, rather than 38 separate network intrusions. The amounts did not appear to correspond with the volume of data allegedly stolen: EUSU Logistics faced a $14m demand for 60mb, with ILCS Pelindo at $2.4m for 2.4gb. Of its 21 earlier victims, SOCRadar said 19 remained at the claimed stage, one was listed as negotiating, and one, Chibitek, had experienced a data leak. SOCRadar warned that maritime businesses that exchange EDI with companies named in the attack should plan for the possibility that their operational data could appear in the 19 October release. It advised them to identify the port community systems, EDI hubs, and file-transfer services handling their data; to check with providers for potential breaches, patch exposed systems, and investigate unusual access or bulk downloads.
